summaries.example: Imagine a team building a house. Different workers do different jobs, but the house can still be one house. Kilwardby used a similar idea for the human soul: growing, sensing, and thinking are different activities, yet they can belong together in one human being.
summaries.summary: Robert Kilwardby was a thirteenth-century philosopher, teacher, church leader, and writer. His work covered logic, grammar, the soul, matter, knowledge, science, and time. He began as a strong reader of Aristotle, especially Aristotle’s logical works, but later became increasingly influenced by Augustine. He continued to interpret Aristotle while trying to make Aristotelian philosophy fit with his Augustinian understanding. A central claim in his philosophy is that the human soul is made up of different forms or abilities. The vegetative form supports life and growth, the sensitive form supports perception, and the intellective form supports thinking. These forms are different, but their ordered relationship can still make one human soul. Kilwardby also argued that perception is not just a passive copy made by an outside object. The object affects a sense organ, while the soul actively forms an inner likeness of what is sensed. Knowledge begins with particular things encountered through the senses. Memory keeps images of these things, and the intellect can find what they have in common, forming universal ideas. Kilwardby also explained how matter and form help account for change and for why things are individual. His writings show a continuing effort to connect philosophy, science, logic, and theology.
key_ideas: Kilwardby was a medieval thinker who studied and taught at Paris and Oxford. He later became a Dominican leader and Archbishop of Canterbury.
He tried to bring together ideas from Aristotle and Augustine instead of simply choosing one and rejecting the other.
He argued that the human soul has vegetative, sensitive, and intellective forms. These support growing, sensing, and thinking.
He thought the soul is active in perception. An object affects the sense organ, but the soul helps form the inner likeness through which the object is perceived.
He held that knowledge begins with particular things sensed by the body and can lead to general ideas in the mind.
He also studied logic, language, science, matter, time, and the organization of different fields of learning.
summaries.why_it_matters: Kilwardby helps us see that medieval philosophy was not only about memorizing old ideas. Thinkers asked difficult questions about how bodies and minds work, how people gain knowledge, and how different sciences fit together. His theory also shows how one philosopher could use Aristotle and Augustine together while disagreeing with other thinkers. Studying him gives us practice in understanding complex arguments without assuming that every disagreement has one simple answer.

important_terms.definition: The part of a living being connected with life. Kilwardby described it as what makes a body alive and able to act.
A basic feature or part that helps make something what it is. Kilwardby said a human soul has several such forms.
The ability to do something that is not active yet but can become active, such as the ability to learn.
The idea that one human soul can include different forms for growing, sensing, and thinking.
The way a thing becomes a particular individual instead of merely belonging to a general kind, such as one particular person.
A general idea, such as ‘human being,’ that can apply to many particular things.

questions_to_think_about: Can something have different parts or abilities and still be one thing?
Is seeing mostly something that happens to us, or does the mind actively help us see?
How might seeing many individual dogs help someone form the general idea ‘dog’?
Why might a thinker want to combine ideas from more than one earlier philosopher?

summaries.example: Consider the difference between seeing a red apple and understanding that apples are fruits. Kilwardby’s account treats perception as an active process: the apple affects the eye through a sensible likeness, while the sensory soul attends to this affection and forms an image. Intellectual cognition then goes further by abstracting a common nature from many particular experiences, allowing the intellect to grasp what apples, or human beings, have in common.
summaries.summary:
Robert Kilwardby was a thirteenth-century English Dominican whose career included teaching at Paris and Oxford, leadership among the English Dominicans, the archbishopric of Canterbury, and finally a cardinalate. His writings range across logic, grammar, theology, natural philosophy, the soul, knowledge, and the classification of sciences. Kilwardby’s philosophical identity is difficult to reduce to a simple label. He began as an Aristotelian commentator, especially on logic, but later became more deeply influenced by Augustine. The entry presents him as an eclectic Aristotelian who sought to harmonize these traditions.

His best-known psychological thesis is the plurality of substantial forms. A human being is a unified composite of body and soul, but the soul itself contains essentially distinct vegetative, sensitive, and intellective forms. The first two arise through natural generation, while the intellective form is created by God and completes the developing human being. Kilwardby argues that these forms must remain distinct because their operations differ: nutrition and growth require bodily processes, sensation requires bodily organs, and understanding does not operate through a bodily organ in the same way. Nevertheless, an ordered plurality can constitute one soul, just as a complex body can remain one body. He therefore opposes theories that make one final form replace or corrupt all previous forms and perform every operation by itself.

Kilwardby’s account of matter includes universal hylemorphism: created things are composed of matter and form, though “matter” can refer differently to bodily and spiritual substances. He treats active potencies as incomplete forms within matter that are directed toward actualization. This helps distinguish natural generation
key_ideas: Kilwardby’s project is synthetic: he remains an interpreter of Aristotle while increasingly adopting Augustinian positions about the soul, perception, and the hierarchy of knowledge.
Against a simple-form theory, he argues that vegetative, sensitive, and intellective operations have different objects and modes of activity, so they must be rooted in essentially different forms.
The plurality of forms does not destroy human unity. The forms are ordered from less complete to more complete, with the intellective form completing the human composite.
In perception, an external object and its likeness affect the sense organ, but the soul is the efficient cause of perception because it attends to the organ’s affection and actively forms an image.
Human cognition begins with singular sensible things. Memory preserves images, experience compares them, and the intellect abstracts a common nature or universal.
Kilwardby explains individuation through both matter and form: matter is the receptive principle, while form actively designates matter as this particular existing thing.
summaries.why_it_matters: Kilwardby’s philosophy matters because it brings together questions that are often separated today: the structure of living beings, the relation between mind and body, perception, abstraction, logic, and the organization of the sciences. His disagreements with rival accounts illustrate how philosophical disputes depend on detailed assumptions about operations, causes, and unity. His theory of perception is especially useful for comparing passive models of sensation with accounts in which the perceiver actively organizes and interprets what is received.

important_terms.definition: A principle that makes a thing what it is. In Kilwardby’s account, the human soul includes essentially distinct vegetative, sensitive, and intellective forms arranged in an ordered unity.
The view that a human being has several substantial forms rather than only one simple form responsible for every operation.
The specifically human form of the soul, associated with understanding and naturally suited to union with a sensory body.
An incomplete or active capacity directed toward its fulfillment in actuality; Kilwardby used it to explain natural change.
The account of how a general nature, such as humanity, is present in individuals and also considered universally by the intellect.
The process by which matter and form together make something a particular individual rather than merely a member of a species.
A likeness or representation through which an object can be known in perception or cognition.
A necessary inference in which a conclusion follows from premises; a demonstration uses suitable principles to produce scientific knowledge.

questions_to_think_about: Does explaining different mental activities require different powers, forms, or kinds of explanation?
Can a composite structure possess genuine unity without being simple?
If an external object is only a necessary occasion for perception, what work remains for the perceiving soul?
Are universals discoveries about shared natures, constructions of the intellect, or both?
What advantages and difficulties follow from treating logic as a general method usable by every science?

summaries.example: Suppose you notice three different dogs at a park. Your senses first meet particular animals: this dog, that dog, and another dog. Your memory keeps images of them. Later, your intellect can notice what they share and form the general idea ‘dog.’ This illustrates Kilwardby’s view that knowledge begins with sensory experience but can rise to universals.
summaries.summary:
Robert Kilwardby was a major English thinker of the thirteenth century. He studied at the University of Paris, taught and studied at Oxford, became a leader of the English Dominicans, and later served as Archbishop of Canterbury and a cardinal. His writings include commentaries on logic and grammar, works on the soul and perception, discussions of matter and individuals, and a large work explaining how the sciences can be organized.

Kilwardby is often connected with Augustinian philosophy, but he never stopped engaging with Aristotle. Early in his career he commented on Aristotle’s logical works. Later, he argued for views that differed from some Aristotelian interpretations of the human soul. His central psychological claim is called the plurality of substantial forms. A human being has a body and a soul, while the soul includes vegetative, sensitive, and intellective forms. The vegetative form supports life processes, the sensitive form supports perception, and the intellective form supports understanding. The first two arise through natural generation, while the intellective form is created by God and completes the human being. Kilwardby believed these forms are genuinely different because their activities and objects differ. Still, they can be united through a natural order, with the intellective form completing the others.

Kilwardby also discussed matter. He described matter as a potential basis that receives forms, and he said that matter can contain active potencies: unfinished capacities directed toward becoming actual. This helped him explain natural change and the development of living things. He used the idea of seminal reasons to explain how the first created beings could contain principles that allow later generations to arise naturally.

key_ideas: Kilwardby worked in the thirteenth century and wrote about logic, grammar, the soul, matter, knowledge, science, and time.
He began with Aristotle but later drew more strongly on Augustine. His goal was often to combine insights from both.
He said the human soul has three important forms: vegetative, sensitive, and intellective.
He believed these forms are different because they have different jobs, but they still form one ordered human soul.
He described perception as partly physical and partly active: an object affects the senses, while the soul helps form an image of what is perceived.
He held that people learn from individual experiences and then use the intellect to understand common features or universals.
summaries.why_it_matters: Kilwardby matters because he shows how philosophers can disagree about a question while sharing many starting points. He accepted the importance of Aristotle but interpreted the soul, perception, and knowledge differently from some of his contemporaries. His work also connects everyday experiences—seeing, remembering, learning, and classifying things—to larger questions about what minds are and how knowledge is possible.

important_terms.definition: The part of the soul connected with basic life activities such as growing and taking nourishment.
The part of the soul connected with sensing and responding through bodily organs.
The part of the soul connected with understanding and reasoning.
A basic feature that helps make a thing the kind of thing it is.
The idea that a human soul contains several substantial forms that work together in an ordered way.
A general nature or idea that can apply to many individuals, such as ‘animal’ or ‘human.’
A capacity that is not fully active yet but is directed toward becoming actual.
A chain of reasoning in which a conclusion follows from stated premises.

questions_to_think_about: Why might different activities, such as digesting and thinking, need different powers?
Can a thing be made of several important parts and still count as one thing?
What is the difference between noticing one dog and understanding the general idea ‘dog’?
Should the mind be viewed as mainly receiving information or also actively shaping it?
Why would logic be useful in many different subjects?
